title: Patient Accounts, Charges, Payments, and Adjustments

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose and components of a patient account and its role in the revenue cycle.
- Post charges, payments, and adjustments accurately to patient accounts following office policy.
- Explain how charges, payments, and adjustments each affect an account balance.
- Recognize discrepancies, credit balances, and unusual account activity and escalate them to qualified staff.
- Apply reconciliation and cash-handling safeguards when processing patient payments.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a patient account like a store's running tab: every time something is charged, money comes in, or a discount is given, it is written down on one page so you always know what is still owed.

### Question 2

A patient account is like a report card for money: it tells you exactly what was billed, what was paid, and what is left over.

### Question 3

Just like every student has a different locker number so books do not get mixed up, each patient has a unique account number so money records never get mixed up.

### Question 4

A guarantor is like the person who promises to pay the restaurant bill for the table, even if someone else at the table ordered the food.

### Question 5

When a child gets a library card, the parent signs for it. A child's medical account works the same way: the account is in the child's name, but the grown-up is responsible for it.

### Question 6

The superbill is like the receipt from a repair shop: it lists exactly what work was done so the office knows what to charge.

### Question 7

A ledger is like a bank statement: every deposit and withdrawal is listed so you can see how the total changes step by step.

### Question 8

A medical record is like a health diary, while the account is like a piggy bank log. One tracks how the person is cared for, and the other tracks the money.

### Question 9

If a cashier types the wrong price, the customer is unhappy and stops trusting the store. The same happens when an office posts a payment to the wrong bill.

### Question 10

If you do not have a coupon to pay for your snack, you pay full price out of your own pocket. A self-pay patient pays the bill the same way.

### Question 11

Adding a charge is like adding an item to a shopping cart: the total goes up.

### Question 12

Posting a payment is like paying down a loan: the amount you still owe gets smaller.

### Question 13

An adjustment is like a coupon that lowers your final total at the store; the amount you owe goes down.

### Question 14

Start with the full price, take away what was paid, then take away the discount, and what is left is what is still owed.

### Question 15

The EOB is like the store's detailed receipt that shows the price, the discount, and what was actually paid.

### Question 16

When someone hands you money for their visit, you write it down as money received and give them a receipt, just like a cashier would.

### Question 17

If a cashier scans your item twice, they remove the extra charge. The office must fix a double charge the same way so the patient pays only once.

### Question 18

If a letter is put in the wrong mailbox, you move it to the right one rather than writing a second letter. A payment posted to the wrong account is fixed the same way.

### Question 19

If you pay a store $20 for a $15 item, the store owes you $5 back. A negative balance means the office owes the patient money back.

### Question 20

If a store agrees to give members a discount, the difference between the full price and the member price is written off; that discount is the contractual adjustment.

### Question 21

A contractual adjustment is a discount the store must give because of its membership rules, while a courtesy adjustment is a discount the manager chooses to give to be nice.

### Question 22

Just like only the manager can decide to erase a customer's bill, only the right people in the office can decide to write off money that is owed.

### Question 23

A debit is like adding to a list of what you owe, and a credit is like crossing things off that list.

### Question 24

The date of service is the day you visited the doctor, and the posting date is the day the office typed it into the computer, which might be a day or two later.

### Question 25

A fee schedule is like the price list on a menu: it tells you how much each service costs.

### Question 26

A lemonade stand keeps its money in a locked box and counts it at the end of the day to make sure nothing is missing; the front desk does the same.

### Question 27

If a store accepts a check that bounces, the purchase is no longer paid for. The office must undo the payment and ask for real money.

### Question 28

When you buy something, you get a receipt to prove you paid. The office gives one for the same reason.

### Question 29

At the end of the day you count the money in the register and check that it matches the receipts, just like balancing a lemonade stand.

### Question 30

If you still owe money from last month's bill, that old amount is carried to the top of this month's bill so nothing is forgotten.

### Question 31

Aging a balance is like checking how long a library book has been overdue to decide how many reminders to send.

### Question 32

When a bill is partly paid by insurance, the leftover part is like the portion you still have to pay after using a gift card; the assistant explains which part is left.

### Question 33

If you are accidentally given too much change, the honest thing is to give it back. The office must return extra payments the same way.

### Question 34

Deductibles and coinsurance are the part of the bill the patient agreed to pay, like paying a share of a shared lunch bill.

### Question 35

When you pay a bill, you mark exactly which purchases are now paid off instead of spreading the money randomly across the receipt.

### Question 36

If a price tag looks wrong, you check the price list and tell the manager instead of quietly changing prices yourself.

### Question 37

Deleting a typo from your homework is a reversal; asking for a small, approved discount is an adjustment. One fixes a mistake, the other reduces a real amount.

### Question 38

A debit adjustment is like discovering an item was left off your bill and adding it back on, so your total goes up.

### Question 39

Money from the patient is like cash handed directly to you, while insurance money comes with a detailed receipt from the company showing what it paid.

### Question 40

A superbill is like the checklist a mechanic gives you showing everything that was done to your car, which is then used to make the bill.

### Question 41

Before ringing up an item, the cashier checks the price tag and that it is the right item. The assistant checks the charge the same way.

### Question 42

If you write in your diary a few days late, you still write the real date the event happened, not today's date.

### Question 43

People pay for a visit the same ways they pay at a store: cash, checks, or cards.

### Question 44

When you make a partial payment on a bill without saying which part, the company applies it to the oldest balance first.

### Question 45

If you find money with no name on it, you put it in a safe place and try to figure out who it belongs to before giving it to someone.

### Question 46

If you paid $5 more than the bill, the store owes you $5. Here the account was paid $50 too much.

### Question 47

A write-off is like a store deciding to forgive a small debt and remove it from your account instead of chasing it.

### Question 48

A payment is real money coming in, while an adjustment is money the office decides not to ask for; labeling one as the other makes the books wrong.

### Question 49

If the cash register does not match the receipts, you do not just make the numbers match; you find out why and tell the manager.

### Question 50

How much money someone owes is private, like a secret; the office keeps it locked up and only shares it with the right people.

### Question 51

Even family members have separate piggy banks; one person's bill is not shown or charged to another grown-up.

### Question 52

You would not record how much money you have based on a guess; you read the actual statement. The office reads the insurance statement before posting.

### Question 53

A monthly bill reminds you what you still owe so you remember to pay, just like a friendly nudge.

### Question 54

When a bill is very overdue, the company sends stronger reminders or asks a collection agency to help; the office follows its own set of steps.

### Question 55

If a customer says a bill is wrong, the store looks into it and asks the manager to decide instead of just erasing the amount.

### Question 56

If the bill was $450 and you paid exactly $450, nothing is left to pay; the account is at zero.

### Question 57

Start with the full bill, subtract the money paid, then subtract the discount, and $80 is left to pay.

### Question 58

The bill is $500, insurance pays $300 and writes off $100, so the patient's share left over is $100.

### Question 59

If your snack costs $30 and you give $50, the cashier gives you $20 back and records only the $30.

### Question 60

Add up all the money that came in from every payment method and you get the total to check against your records.

### Question 61

You paid $50 more than the bill, so the office owes you $50 back.

### Question 62

The full price is $400 but the plan allows only $320, so the $80 difference is the discount the office writes off.

### Question 63

Last month's leftover bill plus this month's new bill together make the full amount you owe now.

### Question 64

The ERA is the electronic version of the insurance company's note explaining exactly what it paid and what it did not.

### Question 65

The bank collects the mail-in money, but the office still has to write each payment down in the correct patient's folder.

### Question 66

If the wrong numbers are written in your notebook, the report you make from it will be wrong too, because it copies the notebook.

### Question 67

Writing things down right away is safer than trying to remember them later, when you might forget or lose the note.

### Question 68

If a store rings up your item on the wrong person's receipt, it moves the item to the right receipt instead of leaving it wrong.

### Question 69

The charge pushes the total up, and the payment and the discount pull it back down; the account shows the combination of all three.

### Question 70

A positive balance is like money still left on your tab: you owe it and need to pay.

### Question 71

An audit trail is like a class sign-in sheet that shows who wrote each entry, so mistakes can be traced back to be fixed.

### Question 72

A reversal is like using an eraser to undo a mistaken line in a math problem so the answer is right again.

### Question 73

Even a tiny leftover amount can only be erased if the manager's rules allow it; the cashier cannot just decide to erase it.

### Question 74

If money keeps not adding up, you tell the person in charge right away instead of waiting or trying to hide it.

### Question 75

The insurance paid $160 of the $200, and the patient's part of the bill is the $40 deductible that is left.

### Question 76

If you deposit $20, you write down $20, not $25, so your notebook matches the real money.

### Question 77

If you owe from two different shopping trips, your payment still counts toward what you owe overall; the store tracks the total honestly.

### Question 78

Erasing money owed without a good reason or permission makes the books wrong, even if everyone is happy about it.

### Question 79

When you fix a mistake in a shared notebook, you write the fix with your name and the date so everyone knows what changed and why.

### Question 80

A bad-debt write-off is when a store gives up collecting from a customer who will never pay, while a contractual adjustment is a discount the store must give because of its rules.

### Question 81

If a customer cannot pay the full amount, the store might offer to split it into smaller payments; the office has similar options to help.

### Question 82

Reconciling is like checking your notebook against the receipts to make sure every number matches before you trust the total.

### Question 83

A zero balance is like a bill that has been fully paid and stamped done; nothing is left to pay.

### Question 84

The assistant follows the approved rules for discounts and asks the manager whenever something looks unusual, instead of deciding on their own.
